original_value: Remote sensing is a promising tool for the detection of floating marine plastics offering extensive area coverage and frequent observations. While floating plastics are reported in high concentrations in many places around the globe, no referencing dataset exists either for understanding the spectral behavior of floating plastics in a real environment, or for calibrating remote sensing algorithms and validating their results. To tackle this problem, we initiated the Plastic Litter Projects (PLPs), where large artificial plastic targets were constructed and deployed on the sea surface. The first such experiment was realised in the summer of 2018 (PLP2018) with three large targets of 10 × 10 m. Hereafter, we present the second Plastic Litter Project (PLP2019), where smaller 5 × 5 m targets were constructed to better simulate near-real conditions and examine the limitations of the detection with Sentinel-2 images. The smaller targets and the multiple acquisition dates allowed for several observations, with the targets being connected in a modular way to create different configurations of various sizes, material composition and coverage. A spectral signature for the PET (polyethylene terephthalate) targets was produced through modifying the U.S. Geological Survey PET signature using an inverse spectral unmixing calculation, and the resulting signature was used to perform a matched filtering processing on the Sentinel-2 images. The results provide evidence that under suitable conditions, pixels with a PET abundance fraction of at least as low as 25% can be successfully detected, while pinpointing several factors that significantly impact the detection capabilities. To the best of our knowledge, the 2018 and 2019 Plastic Litter Projects are to date the only large-scale field experiments on the remote detection of floating marine litter in a near-real environment and can be used as a reference for more extensive validation/calibration campaigns.

result.paraphrase: Remote sensing is a promising method for detecting floating marine plastics because it offers wide-area coverage and frequent observations. Although high concentrations of floating plastics have been reported in many regions worldwide, no reference dataset exists for understanding the spectral behavior of floating plastics in real conditions or for calibrating remote-sensing algorithms and validating their outputs. To address this issue, we launched the Plastic Litter Projects (PLPs), in which large artificial plastic targets were built and placed on the sea surface. The first experiment was carried out in summer 2018 (PLP2018) with three large 10 × 10 m targets. Here, we describe the second Plastic Litter Project (PLP2019), in which smaller 5 × 5 m targets were built to better approximate near-real conditions and to investigate the limits of detection using Sentinel-2 images. The smaller targets and multiple acquisition dates enabled several observations, and the targets were linked in a modular fashion to form different configurations with varying sizes, material compositions, and coverage. A spectral signature for the PET (polyethylene terephthalate) targets was generated by modifying the U.S. Geological Survey PET signature with an inverse spectral unmixing calculation, and this signature was then used to apply matched filtering to the Sentinel-2 images. The results show that, under suitable conditions, pixels with a PET abundance fraction as low as 25% can be successfully detected, while also identifying several factors that significantly affect detection performance. To our knowledge, the 2018 and 2019 Plastic Litter Projects remain the only large-scale field experiments to date on remote detection of floating marine litter in a near-real environment, and they can serve as a reference for larger validation and calibration campaigns.
